title: “Let the Dead Bury Their Dead”
paragraphs:
“Let the Dead Bury Their Dead”
The Shocking Words of Jesus That Still Confront Every Excuse, Every Delay, and Every Divided Heart
There are verses in Scripture that comfort us.
There are verses that heal us.
And then there are verses that stop us in our tracks and leave us staring at the page wondering if Jesus really said what we just read.
This is one of them.
A man approached Jesus with what seemed like a reasonable request.
A compassionate request.
A request that almost everyone reading this would probably approve.
Yet Jesus responded with words so startling that they have echoed through history for two thousand years:
“Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead.”
— Matthew 8:22 (ESV)
At first glance, it feels harsh.
Insensitive.
Almost impossible to reconcile with the Jesus who wept at Lazarus' tomb, welcomed children, healed the brokenhearted, and taught believers to honor their father and mother.
How could the same Savior say something that sounds so cold?
But what if we have misunderstood the scene?
What if Jesus was not diminishing family responsibility at all?
What if He was exposing something far deeper?
Something that still confronts millions of believers today.
Something that may be confronting you right now.
Because hidden inside this short statement is one of the most powerful revelations about discipleship, spiritual life, eternal priorities, and the dangerous temptation to delay obedience.
The deeper meaning may change the way you view your entire walk with Christ.
The account appears in Matthew 8:21-22:
“Another of the disciples said to him, ‘Lord, let me first go and bury my father.’ And Jesus said to him, ‘Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead.’”
The Greek text preserves Jesus' words:
Ἀκολούθει μοι, καὶ ἄφες τοὺς νεκροὺς θάψαι τοὺς ἑαυτῶν νεκρούς
Akolouthei moi, kai aphes tous nekrous thapsai tous heautōn nekrous.
Literally:
“Keep following Me, and allow the dead to bury their own dead.”
Notice something immediately.
Jesus uses the word "dead" twice.
Yet He cannot mean exactly the same thing both times.
Physically dead people cannot bury physically dead people.
So Jesus is speaking on two levels.
The first "dead" refers to those who are spiritually dead.
The second refers to those who are physically dead.
In other words:
"Let those who are spiritually dead handle matters belonging to the realm of physical death. You follow Me."
Suddenly the statement begins to open.
Jesus is not attacking family love.
He is revealing a higher calling.
But there is even more beneath the surface.
Many biblical scholars note that the phrase "let me first bury my father" may not necessarily mean the man's father had just died.
If his father had literally died that day, the disciple likely would not have been standing there listening to Jesus teach.
In first-century Jewish culture, burial happened very quickly.
Many scholars believe the expression often meant:
"Let me stay with my family until my father dies someday, fulfill my responsibilities, receive my inheritance, settle my affairs, and then I will follow you."
If that is true, the conversation suddenly sounds very familiar.
Because it becomes the language of postponement.
The language of "later."
The language of spiritual delay.
The language many of us still speak.
"I'll fully surrender after this season."
"I'll get serious about God once my career is established."
"I'll obey after my finances improve."
"I'll serve when life calms down."
"I'll follow Jesus when the timing is better."
Yet timing never seems to become better.
The enemy rarely tries to convince people to reject Christ outright.
Often he simply convinces them to postpone obedience.
Tomorrow.
Next month.
Next year.
Someday.
The cemetery of lost purpose is filled with people who intended to obey God eventually.
Jesus saw beyond the disciple's words.
He saw the heart.
And He addressed the real issue.
Not family.
Priority.
Not burial.
Allegiance.
Not responsibility.
Delay.
Because Jesus never asked to become one priority among many.
He came demanding first place.
This truth echoes throughout Scripture.
When Jesus said:
“Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me.”
— Matthew 10:37
He was not condemning family love.
He was establishing divine order.
Christ first.
Everything else second.
The Hebrew worldview understood this deeply.
The Hebrew word for heart is:
לֵב (lev)
It represents not merely emotions but the center of will, desire, loyalty, and decision-making.
God has never merely wanted our affection.
He has wanted our lev.
Our deepest allegiance.
Our ultimate loyalty.
Our complete surrender.
The tragedy is that many people want Jesus as Savior but hesitate when He calls as Lord.
We gladly receive forgiveness.
We hesitate at surrender.
We celebrate grace.
We resist obedience.
We love the promise of heaven.
We fear the cost of discipleship.
Yet Jesus never separated the two.
The call to salvation has always included the call to follow.
The Greek word Jesus used:
ἀκολούθει (akolouthei)
means more than walking behind someone.
It means attaching oneself to another person as a disciple.
It means adopting their path, their priorities, their mission, and their life.
Jesus was not inviting casual admiration.
He was calling for complete commitment.
And this is where the passage becomes deeply personal.
Because every believer eventually faces their own version of this conversation.
Not necessarily at a funeral.
But at a crossroads.
The moment where Jesus asks for something costly.
The relationship.
The addiction.
The bitterness.
The secret sin.
The comfort zone.
The fear.
The dream.
The reputation.
The control.
The excuse.
And suddenly we hear ourselves saying:
"Lord, first let me..."
Those three words may be some of the most dangerous words in the Christian life.
"First let me."
Because Jesus never said:
"Handle everything else first and then follow Me."
He said:
"Follow Me."
Now.
Today.
In this moment.
Not after certainty arrives.
Not after fear disappears.
Not after life becomes convenient.
Now.
The reality is that many of us know exactly what God has been asking us to do.
We know the conversation we have avoided.
We know the habit that needs to die.
We know the calling we have delayed.
We know the step of faith we have postponed.
We know the surrender we keep negotiating.
And perhaps that is why this passage feels uncomfortable.
Because Jesus is still speaking.
Still calling.
Still confronting every excuse that hides behind religious language.
Still inviting people out of delay and into discipleship.
Yet before anyone feels condemned, we must remember who is speaking these words.
The One who calls us to follow is the same One who later carried a cross up Calvary.
The same One whose hands were pierced for our sins.
The same One who absorbed the judgment we deserved.
The same One who rose from the grave and conquered death itself.
This is not the demand of a tyrant.
This is the invitation of a Savior.
The One who gave everything asks for everything.
And when He asks for everything, it is because He knows that He Himself is worth more than everything.
This is the beauty of the Gospel.
Jesus does not merely call people away from lesser things.
He calls them into greater life.
The irony is stunning.
The man wanted to attend to death.
Jesus was inviting him into life.
The spiritually dead focus only on earthly realities.
The spiritually alive recognize eternal realities.
The spiritually dead see only what is passing away.
The spiritually alive see the kingdom that cannot be shaken.
Jesus was not minimizing death.
He was announcing that something greater had arrived.
The Kingdom of God was standing right in front of him.
And the same Kingdom stands before us today.
Every day we choose.
Delay or obedience.
Excuses or surrender.
Comfort or calling.
Temporary things or eternal things.
Death or life.
The invitation remains unchanged.
Follow Me.
Not someday.
Today.
Perhaps as you read this, the Holy Spirit is exposing an area where you have been saying, "Lord, first let me..."
Be honest.
What is your "first let me"?
What has been standing between you and complete surrender?
What has been delayed long enough?
Your testimony may encourage someone else who is fighting the same battle.
Someone you know may be standing at the exact crossroads this article describes. Sometimes one shared message becomes the turning point God uses to change a life.
Because every soul reached, every article shared, every truth proclaimed, and every life transformed becomes another testimony that Jesus is still rewriting stories today.
The greatest tragedy is not that Jesus calls us away from the dead.
The greatest tragedy is hearing His voice and choosing to stay where death has already lost.
